stem: A price-taking firm produces Y=L^0.25K^0.25. Labour is hired each week, but capital can be hired only at the start of each month. Wage and capital rental rates both equal 10. The source asks to show that the short-run weekly cost is 10Y⁴/K* with fixed capital K*, and long-run monthly cost is 20Y².
answer: Short-run variable cost is 10Y⁴/K*. Total short-run cost also includes the committed capital cost. Long-run cost is 20Y².
solution:
Raise the production equation to the fourth power. The short-run constraint fixes capital, whereas the long-run problem chooses both inputs; this distinction determines which expenditure is variable.

$$\begin{aligned}
Y^4&=LK,\\
K=K^*&\Longrightarrow L=Y^4/K^*,\\
VC_{SR}(Y)&=10Y^4/K^*,\\
C_{LR}(Y)&=10\min_{LK\ge Y^4}(L+K)
=20Y^2.
\end{aligned}$$

AM–GM proves the long-run lower bound and identifies equality at $L=K=Y^2$. Fixed capital expenditure must be added to short-run variable cost whenever it belongs in the relevant accounting period. The weekly/monthly wording does not itself justify silently deleting a committed cost.

From Y⁴=LK, fixed K=K* requires L=Y⁴/K*. Labour expenditure is therefore 10Y⁴/K*, which is short-run variable cost (or incremental cost after capital has already been paid for). If the rental charge for fixed capital belongs in the accounting period, total short-run cost is 10Y⁴/K*+10K*.

In the long run minimize 10(L+K) subject to LK=Y⁴. AM–GM gives L+K≥2√(LK)=2Y², attained at L=K=Y², so long-run cost is 20Y².

Short-run variable cost is 10Y⁴/K*. Total short-run cost also includes the committed capital cost. Long-run cost is 20Y².
hint: Raise the production equation to the fourth power, then distinguish variable cost from fixed capital cost.
notes: The printed short-run expression omits fixed capital cost and is correctly interpreted as variable/incremental cost. Weekly versus monthly rental accounting is not specified sufficiently for an unqualified total-cost claim.

stem: An IS–LM economy has C=200+0.25Yᴰ, I=150+0.25Y−1000i, G=250, T=200, Yᴰ=Y−T, money demand (m/p)ᵈ=2Y−8000i and real money supply 1600. Find equilibrium values and the new equilibrium after real money supply rises to 1840. Explain the investment effect.
answer: Initially Y=1000, i=0.05, C=400 and I=350. After expansion Y=1040, i=0.03, C=410 and I=380.
solution:
Substitute disposable income into consumption, then collect the two income-induced spending terms. Solve the linear IS–LM pair before evaluating consumption, investment and saving.

$$\begin{aligned}
C&=150+0.25Y,\\
IS:\quad Y&=1100-2000i,\\
LM_0:\quad Y&=800+4000i,\\
(Y_0,i_0)&=(1000,0.05),\\
LM_1:\quad Y&=920+4000i\Longrightarrow(Y_1,i_1)=(1040,0.03).
\end{aligned}$$

The investment change has two components. The lower rate contributes $-1000(-0.02)=20$, while the income increase contributes $0.25(40)=10$. Their sum is $30$, so attributing the entire increase to the interest rate would miss the accelerator channel.

Consumption is C=150+0.25Y. Goods-market clearing gives Y=550+0.5Y−1000i, or Y=1100−2000i. Initial money clearing gives Y=800+4000i.

Solving yields i=0.05 and Y=1000, hence Yᴰ=800, C=400, I=350, G=250 and T=200. Private saving is 400, government saving −50, and national saving 350. With money supply 1840, LM becomes Y=920+4000i.

Its intersection with IS gives i=0.03, Y=1040, Yᴰ=840, C=410, I=380, private saving 430 and national saving 380. The interest-rate fall raises investment directly by 20; the resulting income increase adds 0.25·40=10 of induced investment, for a total rise of 30.

stem: A consumer maximizes U(x,y)=x^α+y^α with α>0 and income M. First suppose prices are equal. Derive demand, and then consider a price of x twice the price of y.
answer: For 0<α<1, demand is interior. For α=1, equal prices give all budget-line bundles as optima. For α>1, equal prices give the two single-good corners. When pₓ=2pᵧ, α≥1 gives x=0 and y=M/pᵧ.
solution:
The exponent controls curvature, so one first-order formula cannot be used for every positive $\alpha$. Separate strictly concave, linear and strictly convex preferences before solving.

$$\begin{aligned}
0<\alpha<1:&\quad (x/y)^{\alpha-1}=p_x/p_y,\\
p_x=p_y=p:&\quad x=y=M/(2p),\\
p_x=2p_y=2p:&\quad r=2^{-1/(1-\alpha)},\\
x&=\frac{rM}{p(1+2r)},\qquad y=\frac{M}{p(1+2r)}.
\end{aligned}$$

For $\alpha=1$, equal prices generate a whole budget line of optima, while unequal prices favor the cheaper good. For $\alpha>1$, utility along the budget is convex, so a maximum occurs at a corner; compare the two corner utilities instead of treating the interior stationary point as a maximum.

Let equal prices be p. If 0<α<1, strict concavity and symmetry give x=y=M/(2p). If α=1, utility is x+y, so every nonnegative bundle with x+y=M/p is optimal.

If α>1, utility is strictly convex along the budget line, and only (M/p,0) and (0,M/p) maximize it. Now let pᵧ=p and pₓ=2p. For 0<α<1 the first-order condition is (x/y)^(α−1)=2.

Set r=2^(−1/(1−α)); then x/y=r and demands are x=rM/[p(1+2r)], y=M/[p(1+2r)]. For α=1 or α>1, spending all income on the cheaper good y is optimal, so x=0 and y=M/p.

For 0<α<1, demand is interior. For α=1, equal prices give all budget-line bundles as optima. For α>1, equal prices give the two single-good corners. When pₓ=2pᵧ, α≥1 gives x=0 and y=M/pᵧ.
hint: Separate the cases of concave, linear, and convex utility before applying first-order conditions.

stem: For Y=L^0.5K^0.5, capital evolves as Kₜ₊₁=(1−δ)Kₜ+Iₜ, with Iₜ=sYₜ. Derive steady-state consumption and find the saving rate that maximizes it.
answer: With fixed L and δ>0, per-worker steady consumption is c*=s(1−s)/δ, maximized at s=1/2. Aggregate consumption is Ls(1−s)/δ.
solution:
Hold labour fixed and express the capital law per worker. At steady state, saving replaces depreciation; consumption is the remaining share of steady output.

$$\begin{aligned}
s\sqrt{k^*}&=\delta k^*,\\
k^*&=(s/\delta)^2,\qquad y^*=s/\delta,\\
c^*(s)&=\frac{s(1-s)}\delta,\\
\frac{dc^*}{ds}&=\frac{1-2s}{\delta},\qquad
\frac{d^2c^*}{ds^2}=-\frac2\delta<0.
\end{aligned}$$

The derivative identifies $s=1/2$, and strict concavity establishes its global optimality. State $\delta>0$ for these positive finite steady-state formulas; if depreciation is zero, positive saving does not produce the same stationary capital level.

With k=K/L, output per worker is √k. The steady-state condition δk=s√k gives k*=(s/δ)² for a positive steady state. Thus y*=s/δ and c*=(1−s)y*=s(1−s)/δ.

Differentiation gives dc*/ds=(1−2s)/δ, so the maximum occurs at s=1/2, with c*=1/(4δ). The second derivative is −2/δ<0. Multiply by the fixed labour force L for aggregate consumption.

With fixed L and δ>0, per-worker steady consumption is c*=s(1−s)/δ, maximized at s=1/2. Aggregate consumption is Ls(1−s)/δ.
hint: Use steady-state investment equals depreciation, then maximize consumption over s.
notes: Assumes fixed labour supply and positive depreciation, as in the stated accumulation equation without population growth.

stem: A is endowed with (x,y)=(25,15), and B with (15,30). The price of y is 1 for buying or selling. The price of x is 1 when selling and 3 when buying. B consumes 20 units of x; A does not trade and consumes her endowment. Could they have the same preferences?
answer: Yes. Both may have utility U(x,y)=x⁴y.
solution:
Transaction prices make each person's budget kink at her own endowment. To prove identical preferences are possible, provide a single utility function that rationalizes both observed choices.

$$\begin{aligned}
U(x,y)&=x^4y,\\
B:\quad3x+y=75&\Longrightarrow (x^*,y^*)=(20,15),\\
A,\ x\le25:\quad x+y=40&\Longrightarrow x_{\rm unconstrained}=32>25,\\
A,\ x\ge25:\quad3x+y=90&\Longrightarrow x_{\rm unconstrained}=24<25.
\end{aligned}$$

For A, each branch's unconstrained optimum lies beyond the branch in the direction of the kink, so both constrained branch maxima occur at the endowment. B instead has an interior optimum on her buying branch. Different choices therefore need not imply different tastes when the two endowment-based budget sets differ.

For B, buying x gives budget 3x+y=3·15+30=75. With utility x⁴y, the optimal purchase bundle is x=(4/5)·75/3=20 and y=15. For A, the endowment kink is (25,15).

On A’s selling branch x≤25, the budget is x+y=40; the unconstrained Cobb–Douglas optimum would be x=32, so the constrained branch maximum occurs at x=25. On A’s buying branch x≥25, the budget is 3x+y=90; the unconstrained optimum would be x=24, so its branch maximum also occurs at x=25. Thus A optimally stays at (25,15), while B optimally buys to reach (20,15), under identical preferences.

Yes. Both may have utility U(x,y)=x⁴y.
hint: Different endowments and a bid–ask price wedge allow identical preferences to produce different trading choices.

stem: A monopolist has cost c(y)=y and demand D(p)=0 for p>20 and D(p)=100/p for 0<p≤20. Find profit-maximizing output with a tax of 1 per unit and the deadweight loss from the tax.
answer: Output remains y=5 and price remains p=20. The additional deadweight loss caused by this tax is zero.
solution:
Invert demand only over the range where positive sales are possible. The maximum permissible demand price makes quantity at least five; ignoring that boundary would give the wrong monopoly choice.

$$\begin{aligned}
p\le20&\Longrightarrow q=100/p\ge5,\\
R(q)&=100,\\
\pi_{\rm taxed}(q)&=100-(1+1)q,\\
q^*_{\rm taxed}&=q^*_{\rm untaxed}=5,\qquad p^*=20.
\end{aligned}$$

The tax lowers profit at every positive quantity but does not change which quantity maximizes it. Since the allocation stays the same, the tax creates no additional deadweight loss. Government receipts are a transfer and must not themselves be counted as destroyed surplus.

A positive sale requires p≤20 and hence y=100/p≥5. Revenue is py=100 for every feasible positive sales level. With marginal cost 1 and per-unit tax 1, profit is 100−2y, maximized at the smallest feasible y=5, corresponding to p=20 and profit 90.

Without the tax, profit 100−y is also maximized at y=5. Quantity and consumers’ price do not change; the tax transfers 5 from the producer to the government without creating an additional quantity distortion. Thus incremental deadweight loss from the tax is 0.

The pre-existing monopoly deadweight loss relative to marginal-cost pricing is a different quantity: ∫₅¹⁰⁰(100/y−1)dy=100ln20−95, and is unchanged by this tax.

stem: A library is located at x∈[0,1]. Consumers A,B,C live at 0.3,0.4,0.6 and have utilities −|x−0.3|, −|x−0.4|, −|x−0.6|. Define Pareto optimality and determine whether x=0.1, 0.3 and 0.6 are Pareto optimal.
answer: x=0.1 is not Pareto optimal. Both 0.3 and 0.6 are Pareto optimal. The full Pareto set is [0.3,0.6].
solution:
Pareto efficiency asks whether any move can benefit someone without hurting anyone, not whether the location minimizes average travel distance. The two extreme residents determine the efficient interval.

$$\begin{aligned}
x<0.3&\Longrightarrow0.3\text{ is closer to all three residents},\\
x>0.6&\Longrightarrow0.6\text{ is closer to all three residents},\\
0.3\le x\le0.6&\Longrightarrow\text{moving left hurts C; moving right hurts A}.
\end{aligned}$$

This proves that the whole interval $[0.3,0.6]$ is efficient. Consequently $0.1$ is dominated, while both $0.3$ and $0.6$ are Pareto optimal even though different people prefer different locations inside the interval.

A location is Pareto optimal if no other feasible location makes every consumer at least as well off and at least one strictly better off. Moving from 0.1 toward 0.3 decreases all three distances, so 0.1 is Pareto dominated. At 0.3, A is at her ideal location, so moving anywhere else makes A worse off; hence 0.3 is Pareto optimal.

Similarly, 0.6 is C’s ideal and is Pareto optimal. More generally, points outside [0.3,0.6] are dominated by the nearest endpoint, while a move from any point inside must hurt at least one of A and C.

stem: An agent has lifetime utility u(c)+βv(d), with increasing concave u,v and 0<β<1. Income is w in period 1 and zero in period 2. The government taxes τw in period 1 and returns T=τw in period 2, with balanced budget. Savings earn interest r. Set up the problem, derive the interior first-order condition, and show that increasing T reduces utility if r>0.
answer: Maximize u(w−T−s)+βv((1+r)s+T). At an interior optimum, u′(c)=β(1+r)v′(d). With r>0, an increase in the balanced-budget transfer lowers lifetime wealth and utility.
solution:
Treat the current tax and future transfer as the same policy variable $T$. Write both consumption amounts in terms of private saving, then compare the present value of resources.

$$\begin{aligned}
c&=w-T-s,\qquad d=(1+r)s+T,\\
u\prime(c)&=\beta(1+r)v\prime(d),\\
c+\frac d{1+r}&=w-\frac{rT}{1+r},\\
\frac{dV}{dT}&=-u\prime(c)+\beta v\prime(d)
=-\frac r{1+r}u\prime(c)<0.
\end{aligned}$$

The government returns the principal without the interest the household could have earned privately. At a positive market return, a larger tax-transfer scheme therefore reduces present-value wealth. The envelope calculation reaches the same conclusion while allowing optimal private saving to adjust.

Let saving be s. Then c=w−τw−s=w−T−s and d=(1+r)s+T. Differentiate the objective with respect to s to obtain −u′(c)+β(1+r)v′(d)=0.

The equivalent lifetime budget is c+d/(1+r)=w−T+T/(1+r)=w−rT/(1+r). Increasing T therefore reduces present-value resources when r>0. Since utility is increasing, optimized utility falls.

At an interior optimum the envelope derivative is dV/dT=−u′(c)+βv′(d)=−[r/(1+r)]u′(c)<0, using the first-order condition.

Maximize u(w−T−s)+βv((1+r)s+T). At an interior optimum, u′(c)=β(1+r)v′(d). With r>0, an increase in the balanced-budget transfer lowers lifetime wealth and utility.
hint: A tax paid now and returned without interest later has a negative present-value effect when r>0.

The envelope calculation reaches the same conclusion while allowing optimal private saving to adjust.

The equivalent lifetime budget is c+d/(1+r)=w−T+T/(1+r)=w−rT/(1+r). Increasing T therefore reduces present-value resources when r>0. Since utility is increasing, optimized utility falls.

stem: A zero-cost monopolist sells X and Y to three consumers with reservation values (X,Y): consumer 1 (4,0), consumer 2 (3,3), consumer 3 (0,4). Each buys at most one unit of each good. Compare separate pricing, pure bundling, and mixed bundling and find the best strategy.
answer: Mixed bundling is best: pₓ=pᵧ=4 and bundle price 6, giving revenue 14 under the usual buy-at-indifference convention. Separate sales and pure bundling each yield at most 12.
solution:
Because production cost is zero, compare revenues. List each consumer's bundle value as the sum of her two reservation values; mixed bundling can extract different values through different purchase options.

$$\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{separate}}^*&=2(2\cdot3)=12,\\
(v_1^{XY},v_2^{XY},v_3^{XY})&=(4,6,4),\\
R_{\mathrm{bundle}}^*&=\max\{3(4),1(6)\}=12,\\
R_{\mathrm{mixed}}&=4+6+4=14.
\end{aligned}$$

The mixed menu serves the two specialist consumers with individual goods and the middle consumer with the bundle. Its revenue equals the sum of all three consumers' maximum total payments, establishing a global upper bound rather than merely a comparison with two candidate strategies.

Separate pricing: each product sells to two consumers at price 3, giving 6 per product and total 12; price 4 gives only 4 per product. Pure bundling: bundle values are 4,6,4, so price 4 sells three bundles and yields 12, while price 6 yields only 6. Mixed bundling: set separate prices at 4 and bundle price at 6.

Consumers 1 and 3 buy their preferred single goods for 4 each; consumer 2 buys the bundle for 6. Revenue is 14, equal to the sum of all consumers’ total reservation values and therefore an upper bound, so this strategy is optimal. If indifferent consumers refuse to buy, choose prices just below these levels and revenue approaches 14.

Mixed bundling is best: pₓ=pᵧ=4 and bundle price 6, giving revenue 14 under the usual buy-at-indifference convention. Separate sales and pure bundling each yield at most 12.
hint: The extreme consumers prefer different single goods; the middle consumer values the bundle more highly.
notes: No production costs are supplied; payoffs are interpreted as revenue. Standard weak participation permits buying at reservation value.

stem: Two consumers each have income M and utility U=xy, where x is restaurant consumption and y is another good. Prices are pₓ,pᵧ. Under plan B they eat together and each pays half the total restaurant bill. Find equilibrium consumption.
answer: In the symmetric Nash equilibrium, each consumes x=2M/(3pₓ) and y=M/(3pᵧ).
solution:
Under a shared bill, an individual chooses her meal while taking the other person's meal as fixed. The private marginal price is half the restaurant price, but the other diner's bill also reduces disposable income.

$$\begin{aligned}
p_yy_i&=M-\frac{p_x}{2}(x_i+x_j),\\
\frac{\partial(x_iy_i)}{\partial x_i}=0
&\Longrightarrow M-p_xx_i-\frac{p_x}{2}x_j=0,\\
x_i= x_j&\Longrightarrow x_i=\frac{2M}{3p_x},\quad y_i=\frac{M}{3p_y}.
\end{aligned}$$

Impose symmetry only after deriving the unilateral best response. The equilibrium spends two-thirds of each budget on restaurant consumption rather than one-half. Each diner ignores the cost imposed on the other, so sharing a bill can lower both people's utility despite appearing cooperative.

If the other consumer chooses xⱼ, consumer i pays (pₓ/2)(xᵢ+xⱼ). Her remaining spending gives yᵢ=[M−(pₓ/2)(xᵢ+xⱼ)]/pᵧ. Maximizing xᵢyᵢ while taking xⱼ as fixed yields M−pₓxᵢ−(pₓ/2)xⱼ=0.

Hence the best response is xᵢ=M/pₓ−xⱼ/2 when positive. Symmetry xᵢ=xⱼ=x gives (3/2)pₓx=M, so x=2M/(3pₓ). Each pays pₓx=2M/3 on the common bill and spends M/3 on the other good, giving y=M/(3pᵧ).

In the symmetric Nash equilibrium, each consumes x=2M/(3pₓ) and y=M/(3pᵧ).

stem: A community owns an exhaustible resource stock X and chooses consumption Cₜ over an infinite horizon to maximize Σδᵗln(Cₜ), where 0<δ<1 and total consumption cannot exceed X. Express optimal Cₜ in terms of δ and X.
answer: With periods indexed t=0,1,…, Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗX. If indexing starts at t=1, Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗ⁻¹X.
solution:
There is one stock constraint across all dates rather than a separate budget each period. Its multiplier is the common shadow value of one extra unit of the resource.

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L&=\sum_{t=0}^\infty\delta^t\log C_t
+\lambda\left(X-\sum_{t=0}^\infty C_t\right),\\
\frac{\delta^t}{C_t}&=\lambda,\qquad
X=\frac1\lambda\sum_{t=0}^\infty\delta^t,\\
C_t^*&=(1-\delta)\delta^tX.
\end{aligned}$$

The geometric allocation equalizes discounted marginal utilities and exactly exhausts the stock. At the surprise date, discard the old plan for future periods but keep past consumption fixed. Apply the same geometric rule to the remaining old stock plus the newly discovered stock, resetting the time index to the discovery date.

The resource constraint binds because log utility is increasing. For a multiplier λ, the first-order condition is δᵗ/Cₜ=λ, so consumption is proportional to δᵗ. For t starting at 0, summing Cₜ=(1/λ)δᵗ gives X=1/[λ(1−δ)], hence Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗX.

If periods start at 1, normalize the geometric weights from t=1 instead; the economically identical path is then Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗ⁻¹X.

With periods indexed t=0,1,…, Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗX. If indexing starts at t=1, Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗ⁻¹X.

notes: The source’s summation has no explicit starting index, so both common indexing conventions are stated. The objective continues on PDF page 13.

stem: With income M and positive prices p₁,p₂, find Marshallian demand for U(x₁,x₂)=max(x₁,x₂) and describe its graph. Then, for U=min(x₁,x₂), find income and own-price elasticities for both goods.
answer: For max utility, buy only the cheaper good; at equal prices the two single-good corners tie. For min utility, x₁=x₂=M/(p₁+p₂), income elasticities are 1 and own-price elasticities are −p₁/(p₁+p₂), −p₂/(p₁+p₂).
solution:
Maximum and minimum utility select opposite geometries. A maximum rewards concentrating spending on one component; a minimum rewards matching every component so that no expenditure is wasted above the bottleneck.

$$\begin{aligned}
\max_i x_i&\le M/\min_jp_j,\\
U=\min_i x_i:&\quad x_i^*=\frac{M}{\sum_jp_j},\\
\eta_{iM}&=\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial M}\frac{M}{x_i}=1,\\
\eta_{ip_i}&=\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_i}\frac{p_i}{x_i}
=-\frac{p_i}{\sum_jp_j}.
\end{aligned}$$

For maximum utility, attain the bound by spending everything on one cheapest good. At a tie, alternative corner bundles maximize utility, but their mixtures generally do not. For minimum utility, differentiate the common quantity formula to obtain elasticities instead of confusing an absolute derivative with a proportional response.

For U=max(x₁,x₂), achieving the largest possible component means spending all income on the cheaper good: if p₁<p₂, demand is (M/p₁,0); if p₂<p₁ it is (0,M/p₂). If prices are equal, precisely the two budget-line corners maximize utility; an interior split gives a smaller maximum component. Holding p₂ fixed, the own-price graph for x₁ follows M/p₁ below p₂, drops to zero above p₂, and has the two possible values {0,M/p₂} at p₁=p₂.

The x₂ graph is analogous. For U=min(x₁,x₂), optimal consumption has equal quantities because excess of either good alone does not raise utility. The budget gives x₁=x₂=M/(p₁+p₂).

Differentiation yields income elasticity 1 for both, and own-price elasticities −p₁/(p₁+p₂) for good 1 and −p₂/(p₁+p₂) for good 2.

stem: An economy has m individuals and aggregate endowments ω₁,…,ωₙ of n goods. Individual i has Uᵢ=∏ⱼ Cⱼⁱ. (a) Define an allocation, a Pareto-inferior allocation, and a Pareto-optimal allocation. (b) Is an allocation Cⱼⁱ=λⁱωⱼ for every j, with nonnegative λⁱ and Σᵢλⁱ=1, Pareto optimal?
answer: Yes: proportional allocations are Pareto optimal for these identical product preferences.
solution:
Normalize each holding by the corresponding aggregate stock. This turns feasibility into a common unit upper bound for every good, making the proportional-allocation proof independent of units.

$$\begin{aligned}
z_j^i&=C_j^i/\omega_j,\qquad\sum_i z_j^i\le1,\\
\prod_jz_j^i&\ge(\lambda^i)^n,\\
\frac1n\sum_jz_j^i&\ge\left(\prod_jz_j^i\right)^{1/n}\ge\lambda^i,\\
\text{a strict Pareto gain}&\Longrightarrow
\frac1n\sum_j\sum_i z_j^i>\sum_i\lambda^i=1.
\end{aligned}$$

AM–GM converts each person's required product utility into a lower bound on her average resource share. A strict gain for anyone makes the aggregate inequality strict, contradicting the normalized feasibility bound. This proves efficiency directly, including consumers assigned zero shares, rather than relying only on tangency conditions.

(a) A feasible allocation assigns Cⱼⁱ≥0 to each person with ΣᵢCⱼⁱ≤ωⱼ for each good. It is Pareto inferior if some feasible allocation makes every person at least as well off and at least one person strictly better off. It is Pareto optimal if no such improvement exists.

(b) Suppose ωⱼ>0 and define normalized shares zⱼⁱ=Cⱼⁱ/ωⱼ. The proposed allocation gives each person utility (λⁱ)ⁿ∏ⱼωⱼ. Any Pareto improvement must satisfy ∏ⱼzⱼⁱ≥(λⁱ)ⁿ for all i, strictly for someone.

By AM–GM, (Σⱼzⱼⁱ)/n≥(∏ⱼzⱼⁱ)^(1/n)≥λⁱ, strictly for that person. Summing over i would then give (1/n)ΣⱼΣᵢzⱼⁱ>Σᵢλⁱ=1, violating feasibility Σᵢzⱼⁱ≤1. Therefore no Pareto improvement exists.

This proof also covers zero λⁱ. If an aggregate endowment is zero, all product utilities are zero and no feasible strict utility improvement is possible.

Yes: proportional allocations are Pareto optimal for these identical product preferences.

stem: A monopolist faces domestic inverse demand p=5−(3/2)qₕ and can sell abroad at constant price 3. Total cost is C(q)=q² with q=qₕ+q𝒻. Foreign sales cannot exceed 1/6. Find optimal domestic and foreign quantities.
answer: Domestic quantity qₕ=14/15; foreign quantity q𝒻=1/6.
solution:
Domestic and export sales share the same total-production cost. When exports are unconstrained, their price sets the marginal revenue to which domestic sales are compared. A binding export ceiling changes that condition.

$$\begin{aligned}
\pi&=(5-1.5q_h)q_h+3q_f-(q_h+q_f)^2,\\
\text{unrestricted: }2(q_h+q_f)&=3,\quad5-3q_h=3,\\
q_f=1/6:&\quad5-3q_h-2(q_h+1/6)=0,\\
q_h&=14/15,\qquad q_h+q_f=11/10.
\end{aligned}$$

First solve the unconstrained allocation and check it against the cap. Because its exports exceed $1/6$, the cap binds. Re-optimize domestic sales with exports fixed at that boundary, then verify the export marginal profit remains positive to confirm that relaxing the cap would help.

Profit is (5−1.5qₕ)qₕ+3q𝒻−(qₕ+q𝒻)². Without the export cap, foreign marginal revenue 3 would imply total quantity 3/2, while domestic MR=5−3qₕ=3 gives qₕ=2/3 and q𝒻=5/6, exceeding the cap. Thus the cap binds: q𝒻=1/6.

The domestic first-order condition is 5−3qₕ−2(qₕ+1/6)=0, giving qₕ=14/15. At this point total quantity is 11/10 and foreign marginal profit is 3−2·11/10=4/5>0, confirming the desire to export more if allowed. The profit Hessian is negative definite, so this constrained solution is the unique maximum.

Domestic quantity qₕ=14/15; foreign quantity q𝒻=1/6.

stem: An economy produces F=√(L𝒻T) and M=√(LₘK), with mobile labour L𝒻+Lₘ=100, K=36, T=49 and both output prices 1. Landlords own land and capitalists own capital. (a) Find sectoral labour allocation. (b) If land is unowned and available free, find the new allocation.
answer: (a) L𝒻=980/17 and Lₘ=720/17. (b) Under open-access self-employment on unowned land, L𝒻=2450/29 and Lₘ=450/29.
solution:
Owned land rewards hired labour at its marginal product. Under open access, a self-employed entrant keeps average product instead, creating an externality on other food workers.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{private land: }\frac7{2\sqrt{L_F}}&=\frac6{2\sqrt{L_M}}
\Longrightarrow\frac{L_F}{L_M}=\frac{49}{36},\\
\text{open access: }\frac7{\sqrt{L_F}}&=\frac3{\sqrt{L_M}}
\Longrightarrow\frac{L_F}{L_M}=\frac{49}{9},\\
L_F+L_M&=100.
\end{aligned}$$

Use each ratio together with the labour endowment to recover levels. At common unit output prices, total output is a transparent efficiency criterion, though it is not a complete distributional welfare function. Comparing the two totals shows the cost of excessive entry into food production.

(a) Competitive labour mobility equates marginal products: 7/(2√L𝒻)=6/(2√Lₘ). Hence L𝒻/Lₘ=49/36. Together with total labour 100, this gives L𝒻=4900/85=980/17 and Lₘ=3600/85=720/17.

(b) Under the common-property/open-access interpretation, a worker entering food production receives average food product F/L𝒻=7/√L𝒻 because no landlord collects rent. Manufacturing still pays marginal product 3/√Lₘ. Mobility therefore gives 7/√L𝒻=3/√Lₘ, so L𝒻/Lₘ=49/9 and L𝒻=4900/58=2450/29, Lₘ=900/58=450/29.

Open access attracts excessive labour into food relative to the private-land allocation.

(a) L𝒻=980/17 and Lₘ=720/17. (b) Under open-access self-employment on unowned land, L𝒻=2450/29 and Lₘ=450/29.
hint: With owned land compare marginal products; with open-access self-employment compare food average product to the manufacturing wage.
notes: Part (b) uses the standard open-access/common-property interpretation of unowned land. Merely waiving a land rental payment while retaining competitive firms and exclusive fixed land access would not, by itself, replace marginal-product wage setting. The data and part (b) continue on PDF page 14.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the problem
solutionSteps.body: Owned land rewards hired labour at its marginal product. Under open access, a self-employed entrant keeps average product instead, creating an externality on other food workers.

solutionSteps.title: Work through the equations
Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
(a) Competitive labour mobility equates marginal products: 7/(2√L𝒻)=6/(2√Lₘ). Hence L𝒻/Lₘ=49/36. Together with total labour 100, this gives L𝒻=4900/85=980/17 and Lₘ=3600/85=720/17.

(b) Under the common-property/open-access interpretation, a worker entering food production receives average food product F/L𝒻=7/√L𝒻 because no landlord collects rent. Manufacturing still pays marginal product 3/√Lₘ. Mobility therefore gives 7/√L𝒻=3/√Lₘ, so L𝒻/Lₘ=49/9 and L𝒻=4900/58=2450/29, Lₘ=900/58=450/29.

Open access attracts excessive labour into food relative to the private-land allocation.

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: (a) L𝒻=980/17 and Lₘ=720/17. (b) Under open-access self-employment on unowned land, L𝒻=2450/29 and Lₘ=450/29.

stem: A domestic economy starts with Y₀=100 and C₀=I₀=S₀=50. Investment is autonomous. Each year’s expenditure determines that year’s income and Cₜ=0.5Yₜ₋₁. A foreign country lends 100 in year 1 at zero interest, only for investment, repayable at the beginning of year 2. Find income, consumption, investment and saving in years 1 and 2 and in the final equilibrium if the loan is taken in year 1 only.
answer: Under a net-autonomous-expenditure convention: year 1 (Y,C,I,S)=(200,50,150,150); year 2 (50,100,−50,−50); final equilibrium (100,50,50,50). The year-2 investment figure is net of loan repayment, so this interpretation needs to be stated.
solution:
Keep consumption lagged one period, and state explicitly the conditional net-expenditure convention used to translate borrowing and repayment into demand. Principal repayment is not itself an output transaction.

$$\begin{aligned}
J_1&=50+100=150,\quad C_1=0.5(100)=50,\\
Y_1&=200,\quad S_1=150,\\
J_2&=50-100=-50,\quad C_2=0.5(200)=100,\\
Y_2&=50,\quad S_2=-50,\\
t\ge3:&\quad Y_t=0.5Y_{t-1}+50\longrightarrow100.
\end{aligned}$$

The year-two fall is conditional on repayment withdrawing one hundred from expenditure. Without a specified repayment-financing mechanism, ordinary gross investment need not become negative. Once the exceptional loan flows cease, the stable lagged-consumption recurrence brings output back toward its original level.

A common intended expenditure model is Yₜ=Cₜ+Jₜ, where Jₜ=50+new loan−principal repayment. Then J₁=150, C₁=0.5·100=50, so Y₁=200 and S₁=150. In year 2, C₂=0.5·200=100 and J₂=50−100=−50, giving Y₂=50 and S₂=−50.

For t≥3, Jₜ=50 and Yₜ=0.5Yₜ₋₁+50, so Y converges to 100 and C,I,S converge to 50. However, repayment of principal is a financial transaction, not automatically negative gross investment or a subtraction from GDP. If I is meant as ordinary gross investment fixed autonomously at 50 after year 1, the problem must specify how repayment is financed and how it changes expenditure; the quoted year-2 values cannot be asserted from national accounting alone.

Hence the numerical table above is conditional on interpreting I as net autonomous spending including the repayment withdrawal.

Under a net-autonomous-expenditure convention: year 1 (Y,C,I,S)=(200,50,150,150); year 2 (50,100,−50,−50); final equilibrium (100,50,50,50). The year-2 investment figure is net of loan repayment, so this interpretation needs to be stated.
